## Background

I'm Frederick Abalo, a geospatial software engineer from Ghana. My work connects spatial data with the services and tools that people use to manage it: APIs, processing pipelines, mapping applications, and quality checks.

At **Zipline**, I worked on geospatial systems supporting autonomous medical delivery. My experience includes building internal applications for spatial-data ingestion and validation, developing Python pipelines orchestrated with Prefect, working with PostgreSQL/PostGIS data models, and supporting services on AWS and Kubernetes. I also worked on imagery and terrain processing, mapping QA, and route-planning workflows, alongside engineering and operations teams.

That work combined software development with production support: investigating failures, improving repeatable workflows, and making spatial data usable by other teams. Employer source code, internal screenshots, and operational datasets are not included in this portfolio.

I own **[Geomersive](https://geomersive.org)** and work on its spatial-data application, including dataset and product catalogs, upload workflows, mapping viewers, and processing workers. The main application remains private and under development. The [public tile utilities](https://github.com/GeomersiveTeam/geomersive-tile-utils) are a smaller example of the mapping code I maintain.

Earlier roles included GIS analysis, satellite-image interpretation, field data collection, and mapping for sanitation and agricultural projects. My undergraduate degree is a **BSc in Geomatic Engineering from the University of Mines and Technology**.

## Education and current focus

I'm pursuing the **Master of Urban Spatial Analytics at the University of Pennsylvania**, with expected graduation in **May 2027**. At Penn, I'm extending my work in statistics, spatial modeling, urban systems, and reproducible analysis with R and Quarto.

I'm interested in geospatial software, mapping infrastructure, and backend engineering roles where data quality, system reliability, and clear interfaces matter.
